subject: Autoscaling & burst-capacity follow-up — latency SLOs, warm pools, next steps
messages:
From: Sergio Alvarez <sergio@redwood.ai>
To: Samantha Li <samantha@finflow.io>, Devon Park <devon.park@finflow.io>
Cc: Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-03-11T09:15:00-07:00
Subject: Autoscaling follow-up: call recap and a couple of clarifying questions

Hi Samantha / Devon —

Thanks again for the time today. Quick recap from my side so we have a shared baseline and clear next steps:

Summary of what I heard on the call:
- Primary SLO: 95th percentile end-to-end response latency for streaming responses <= 250ms (soft), 99.9p <= 750ms (hard).
- Expected steady-state throughput: ~1,200 req/min (~20 rps) across a handful of front-end services.
- Typical concurrency: 60–90 active concurrent streams during business hours; peak bursts up to ~450 concurrent for short windows (3–8 minutes) during product events.
- Streaming behavior: partial token streaming acceptable; clients can tolerate a few partial updates as long as first-byte latency remains low.

Call items / open questions for us to confirm:
1) Burst SLA expectations: you mentioned a "burst to 500" target — can you confirm whether that is an absolute hard burst requirement or a desired target we should try to meet with best-effort fallbacks?
2) Warm pool tolerance: would you prefer a moderately-sized warm pool (pre-warmed workers ready to accept requests immediately) to keep first-byte latencies low, or do you want to optimize purely for cost and accept a slightly higher scale-up window?
3) Queueing preference: when capacity is constrained, do you want requests queued for up to X seconds (please specify) or prefer immediate 429s/fail-fast so upstream can backoff?

Next steps I propose: 
- Marcus and I will model a warm-pool sizing suggestion and expected scale-up curve (cold vs warm) and send a short SLO/queueing matrix.
- We’ll put together a short load-test plan and recommend an initial test window next week (we can run a small Canary load into a dedicated pool for FinFlow).
- Share a draft mutual action plan + timing and a link to the test dashboard.

I attached a one-page SLO matrix draft as a starting point; Marcus will follow up with more engineering detail.

Thanks — talk soon.

Best,
Sergio
Enterprise Sales
Redwood Inference

From: Samantha Li <samantha@finflow.io>
To: Sergio Alvarez <sergio@redwood.ai>
Cc: Devon Park <devon.park@finflow.io>
Date: 2026-03-11T11:02:00-07:00
Subject: Re: Autoscaling follow-up: call recap and a couple of clarifying questions

Hi Sergio —

Appreciate the recap — that looks accurate. A few clarifications from our side:

- Burst requirement: We need a best-effort guarantee to handle up to 500 concurrent streams for at least 5 minutes during a product push. If that can't be guaranteed, we need a documented fallback (e.g., reduced quality model variant or regional failover).
- Queueing: prefer short queueing (up to 8s) to avoid client-side timeouts; after that we prefer 429s so our front-end can surface an informative retry.
- Streaming: first-byte latency is the highest priority — if streaming partial tokens helps keep first bytes under the soft SLO, that's fine.

Can you confirm your expected scale-up window from a cold start vs from a warm pool, and what warm-pool sizes you recommend for our traffic profile?

We are available for the load test next Tuesday or Thursday (PDT).

Thanks,
Samantha
Director, Platform Engineering
FinFlow

From: Marcus Lin <marcus_lin@redwood.ai>
To: Sergio Alvarez <sergio@redwood.ai>, Vivek Kulkarni <vivek_kulkarni@redwood.ai>, Marissa Cole <marissa_cole@redwood.ai>
Date: 2026-03-11T15:30:00-07:00
Subject: RE: Autoscaling follow-up: call recap and a couple of clarifying questions

Sergio / team —

Following up with concrete numbers and a proposed approach after reviewing FinFlow's targets:

Scale behavior (measured & expected):
- Cold start (no warm pool): full worker initialization + model warmup averages ~110–140s depending on model size and quantization. First-byte can be delayed during that window.
- Minimal warm pool (pre-warmed runtimes, no model loaded): ~45–60s to be fully ready for high-throughput streaming; first-byte still impacted until model weights are loaded into GPU memory.
- Pre-loaded warm pool (model loaded into memory, weights pinned to GPUs): ~8–15s to accept streaming requests at low latency (this is what we recommend for aggressive first-byte SLOs).

Warm-pool sizing guidance for your profile (1,200 req/min baseline, peaks to 450–500 concurrent):
- Baseline reserved (steady-state): capacity to support 80 concurrent streams.
- Warm pool (pre-loaded): keep ~25% of peak concurrent (~120 pre-loaded streams) which lets us absorb most short spikes without queuing; additional nodes can be brought up behind an autoscaler in ~12–45s depending on hardware locality.
- Cold burst headroom: for multi-minute sustained bursts above warm-pool capacity we recommend a short queue (configurable up to 8s per Samantha) + a fallback routing policy to a cheaper quantized model variant if scale doesn't catch up within 30s.

Queue & backpressure behavior:
- Default: we support request-level queuing with bounded queue size and configurable timeout; recommend queue timeout = 8s for FinFlow. After timeout, requests return 429 with a Retry-After header.
- Token-level throttling: we can limit tokens/sec per connection during mass bursts to avoid long tails for other customers on the same pool.

Recommendations / trade-offs:
- For strict first-byte 95p <= 250ms, pre-loaded warm pool is required; cost increases but peak user experience will be preserved.
- If cost is a primary concern, we can reduce warm-pool size to 60–80 preloaded streams and rely on a brief queue + model-variant fallback for rare large bursts.

I attached a short SLO matrix and a warm-pool diagram. If agreed, we can sketch the initial load-test plan: 30-minute window, ramp to 500 concurrent for 5 minutes, validate 95p/99.9p latencies and fallbacks.

—Marcus
Senior Engineering Manager, Serving Runtime
Redwood Inference

Mutual action plan (MAP) — proposed timeline:
1) Today: engineering note & attachments sent (slo_matrix_v1.xlsx, warm-pool-diagram.png) — done.
2) Tue 2026-03-17: Canary load test (30 min) — Redwood to run ramp to 500 concurrent for 5 minutes; FinFlow to provide representative sample prompts and the front-end test harness.
3) Wed 2026-03-18: Post-test review — analyze 95p/99.9p latencies, queue timeout behavior, and fallback effectiveness.
4) Week of 3/22: Production rollout plan (if test passes) — decide on warm-pool size (our baseline recommendation: 120 pre-loaded streams) and production autoscaler policy.

Action items — who does what:
- FinFlow: confirm the representative prompt set and API client behavior (timeouts/retry logic) by EOD Monday.
- Redwood (Marcus): finalize warm-pool sizing and test configuration and share load-test dashboard link.
- Redwood (Sergio): schedule the Canary window and send the HubSpot deal + test dashboard links.

Attachments: slo_matrix_v1.xlsx, warm-pool-diagram.png
Links: HubSpot deal and internal load-test dashboard (shared above).

If this looks good I’ll lock the Tues/Thu test windows — you said Tue or Thu, so I’ll hold Tue 3/17 10:00–10:45 PT tentatively until you confirm.

Thanks — really appreciate the clear SLOs; we’ll make sure engineering runs the right validation and we capture the fallbacks in the runbook.

Best,
Sergio
